title: Channels two and three: saying so, and oiling the wheels

cues.text: The second channel does not need the money to go anywhere at all. It works purely through what the action tells everybody.
By loosening policy this much, the Bank is saying it expects to keep rates low for a long time yet.
It is revealing its own reading of how bad things are.
And by acting at all, it is showing that it is still committed to its target, and still confident it can hit it — even down at the floor.
Which helps keep people's expectations of future inflation anchored. And expectations, as chapter twenty-five will show, are themselves a lever.
liquidity. How easily you can sell it.
When markets seize up, you may not be able to find a buyer at all. So investors demand a higher return to compensate them for that risk.
liquidity premium. The extra return for maybe not being able to sell.
A central bank buying on a very large scale is, among other things, a buyer. It puts trading back into the market, and that premium comes down.
But the authors are careful about this one. The effect probably lasts only while the purchases are going on. And in gilt markets, which are normally very liquid anyway, it may be small.
Here is what the research can see. Government bond yields fell after the purchases. Company bond yields fell. Share prices rose.
And here is what it cannot see. Which of those three channels did it. They are very hard to tell apart, and the authors say so.
There is also disagreement about how big those effects were and how long they lasted. And the effects on wider classes of assets are less marked than on company bonds.
